transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I'm here because I'm just... I'm so worn down by all of it. For the last year, I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or, like, holding back parts of my dad’s lab results. And I know labs. I’m a phlebotomist, actually. I was just working yesterday and had this guy with the most difficult rolling veins—took me three tries with a butterfly needle, which I hate doing because they always bruise, and then the patients get so mad at you, you know? People are so particular about their arms. 

But anyway, I know what blood work is supposed to look like. No matter how many doctors or even my own family members tell me his numbers are fine, I know the chart doesn’t match what I originally saw. I saw it with my own eyes. Just like I saw the new holiday schedule they posted in the breakroom at my work, which is completely unfair by the way, because they gave me the early shift on Christmas Eve again. And the coffee machine in there has been broken since Tuesday, so everyone is already in a terrible mood. 

But yeah, no one will listen to me about the results. It's just exhausting me, trying to get someone to see that the numbers were changed.

When the doctors and your family tell you that your dad's lab numbers are fine, do you think they might actually be right and you could be mistaken, or are you completely certain that the numbers were changed?

Mistaken? No. No, absolutely not. I am one hundred percent completely certain they were changed. I know what I saw. 

Because I know how these portals work, you know? We use a similar electronic system at my clinic, and usually, everything leaves a trace. Like, just last week, my coworker Sarah—she accidentally deleted a whole batch of patient labels. It was a complete disaster. We had to reprint all of them, and the printer on our floor is ancient. It makes this horrible, high-pitched squealing sound every time it feeds a sheet of paper, which practically gives me a migraine. I’ve told management to replace it like five times, but they always say it's not in the budget. They can spend money on catered Panera lunches for the executives every Friday, but they can't buy us a new printer for the lab. It makes no sense.

But... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, my dad's labs. Yeah, no, I am definitely not wrong. My family and the doctors, they just don't want to deal with the hassle of investigating it, or they just don't understand how easy it is to alter a record if you have the right admin access. I saw the original numbers with my own eyes. I know the chart doesn't match what I originally saw, and they are definitely holding parts of it back. It's just wearing me down to nothing trying to get anyone to admit it.
You mentioned this has been going on for about a year with your dad's lab results. Did these beliefs and concerns about the lab results start suddenly, or did they develop gradually over time?

It was about a year ago. That’s exactly when his medical problems really started getting worse, so he was suddenly requiring all these frequent labs and appointments. And I know all about frequent appointments because I swear half the patients at my clinic are frequent flyers. We have this one lady, Mrs. Higgins, who comes in every single Tuesday for her blood draws. Every Tuesday. And she always brings these hard butterscotch candies, which is sweet of her, I guess, but she leaves the sticky little wrappers everywhere. I found one stuffed in the dirt of the fake ficus plant in the waiting room yesterday. I mean, who does that? There’s a trash can literally two feet away. 

It’s just like how people leave their grocery carts in the middle of the parking lot instead of returning them to the corral. My car actually got a huge scratch on the passenger side last month because some guy just shoved his cart away and the wind caught it. A huge, deep scratch right on the door of my Civic. The body shop quoted me six hundred dollars to fix it, which I just don't have right now because rent went up again. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, my dad. Yeah, it was about a year ago when all his medical issues started and he had to go in for all those frequent tests. That's when I started seeing what they were doing.
Besides the lab results, have you been hearing voices or seeing things that other people around you don't seem to notice or hear?

Voices? No, I'm not crazy. I don't hear voices or see ghosts or whatever you're asking. I just see the numbers on the screen. Like I said, I know what I'm looking at. It's just data. 

Speaking of data, you wouldn't believe the new software update they pushed to our clinic's system over the weekend. It completely messed up the interface. Before, the patient's date of birth was right at the top left, in bold, so you could verify it in two seconds. Now? Now you have to click this tiny little drop-down arrow on the right side, scroll past their emergency contacts, and it's buried at the bottom. I almost drew blood from the wrong John Smith on Monday because of it. Thank god I asked him to state his birthday out loud, which is protocol, obviously, but still. 

And don't even get me started on the new barcode scanners. They are so sensitive. If the room is too bright, it won't scan the vial. I had to literally stand in the corner of the room, blocking the overhead light with my body, just to scan a lipid panel. The patient was looking at me like I was doing some kind of weird dance. I swear, the people who design these things have never actually worked in a lab a day in their lives. They just sit in their fancy offices and... 

Wait, what did you ask me? Oh, right, voices. No. No voices. Just the lab results. I just want someone to look at the actual lab results.

When you first started noticing that the lab results were being changed a year ago, did this realization come to you suddenly—like something just clicked and you suddenly knew what was happening—or did you gradually become more and more convinced over weeks or months?

Well, it wasn't like a lightbulb went off or anything. I don't really know if it was sudden or gradual, to be honest. I just know what I saw. 

It kind of reminds me of when I realized my ex-boyfriend was stealing from my purse. I didn't just wake up one day and know he was doing it. It was just little things, you know? Like, I'd have a twenty-dollar bill in my wallet on Tuesday, and by Thursday, it was gone. And I knew I hadn't bought anything because I bring my own lunch to work. I always make a turkey sandwich on wheat bread, with a little bit of mayo and some spinach. The spinach keeps better than lettuce, it doesn't get all soggy by noon. Plus, it has more iron, which is important. We see so many anemic patients at the clinic. They come in looking so pale, and you just know their hemoglobin is going to be in the basement. 

I actually tried to get my ex to eat more spinach, but he was one of those guys who refused to eat anything green. He practically lived on frozen pizzas and energy drinks. It was disgusting. His apartment always smelled like stale pepperoni and cheap cologne. I don't even know why I stayed with him as long as I did. He didn't even have a real job, he just did "freelance graphic design," which basically meant he played video games all day while I was at the clinic drawing blood for eight hours. 

But... wait. What were you asking me? Oh, about the labs. Yeah, I don't really know if it was sudden or not. I just started noticing the numbers didn't match what I saw originally. That's all.

Over this past year while you've been dealing with the lab results situation, have you noticed any changes in how you're sleeping, or have you felt unusually energized or restless, or experienced any confusion with your thoughts?

My sleep? No, I sleep fine. I'm not restless or confused or anything like that. I actually sleep pretty well since I got that new memory foam mattress a few months ago. It's one of those bed-in-a-box ones they just leave on your porch. Though, honestly, the delivery driver just dumped it at the bottom of the stairs of my apartment building. I had to drag this eighty-pound box up two flights of stairs by myself. 

I asked my downstairs neighbor, Greg, if he could give me a hand, but he just pretended he didn't hear me. He's always wearing those giant noise-canceling headphones. He works from home doing something with IT, I think, but I swear he just plays video games all day because I can hear the bass from the explosions through my floorboards. I've complained to the landlord about it three times, but she doesn't do anything. She's too busy repainting the exterior of the building this hideous shade of mustard yellow. It literally looks like baby poop. I don't know who picked that color, but they clearly have no taste. I told the property manager they should have gone with a nice slate gray, it's so much more modern. We actually just painted the breakroom at the clinic slate gray and it looks so clean. It hides the coffee stains on the wall, too, because Dr. Aris always bumps the trash can when he throws his cups away and it splashes. 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, my thoughts. No, my thoughts are completely clear. I'm not confused at all. I just want to know why his lab numbers are being changed. That's it. But my sleep and my energy, they're just normal.

I've noticed that during our conversation, you sometimes start talking about one thing—like your dad's labs—and then jump to talking about other things like your coworker Sarah, the printer, or your ex-boyfriend. Do you notice yourself doing that, or does it feel like everything you're saying is all connected and related?

Connected? Well, yeah, of course it's connected. I'm just trying to give you the full picture. If I don't give you the background, you won't understand what's actually going on. It's like when I have to explain to a patient why they need to fast before a metabolic panel. You can't just tell them not to eat. You have to explain why, because otherwise they'll just go through the drive-thru at Starbucks and get one of those giant caramel frappuccinos. 

Do you know how much sugar is in one of those? It's insane. My coworker, Sarah, gets a venti iced coffee every single morning, and she always leaves the cup sweating on the counter right next to the centrifuge. I've told her a hundred times that the condensation is going to mess up the barcodes on the specimen tubes, but she just rolls her eyes. She has absolutely no respect for the equipment. That centrifuge cost the clinic like three thousand dollars. It's a really good one, too, it spins down a gold-top tube in five minutes flat. Our old one used to take ten minutes and it made this horrible screeching noise the whole time. It sounded exactly like my neighbor's cat when it gets locked out on the balcony in the rain. I feel so bad for that cat, I've actually tried leaving little salmon treats out for it on my windowsill, but the pigeons always get to them first. Pigeons are basically just rats with wings, honestly. They carry so many diseases. 

Wait, what were you asking me? Did I jump topics? No, I'm just explaining the context. It all makes sense to me, I'm just trying to make sure you get the whole story so you can see what's happening with the lab numbers.

When you're talking and you move from one topic to another—like going from the lab results to the printer to the coffee machine—do you feel like your thoughts are racing really fast and you can't slow them down, or does it feel normal to you, just like you're giving me details?

Racing? No, not at all. My thoughts aren't going fast or anything. It just feels completely normal to me. I'm just trying to be thorough with the details. You really have to be detail-oriented, you know? Especially in my line of work. If you miss one little detail on a patient's chart, or if you write the wrong time of draw on a lavender-top tube, the whole thing gets rejected by the lab. 

We actually had this courier from the main lab come in last week to pick up the afternoon samples, and he was completely clueless. He dropped an entire rack of urine cups. Thank God the lids were screwed on tight. I always make sure to double-check the lids because patients never put them on right. They always cross-thread them. It's like people don't know how a screw-top works anymore. It reminds me of those jars of artisan pickles my sister buys. She gets them from this farmer's market downtown, the one where everything is ridiculously overpriced. Like, eight dollars for a jar of pickles? And they always put this weird wax seal on top that you have to chip away with a butter knife just to open it. I chipped my favorite coffee mug doing that once. It was this mug I got from a phlebotomy conference in Orlando. Orlando is way too humid, honestly. My hair was just frizz the entire time I was there. I couldn't even use the hotel straightener because the plug was all weird and loose in the wall. It's a huge fire hazard, if you ask me.

Anyway... wait, what was the question? My thoughts? Yeah, no, they aren't racing. I'm just giving you the details so you understand. Everything is just normal speed.

Before this year when you started noticing the lab results being changed, would you say that a year ago you were functioning pretty normally at work and in your personal life, or had you already been struggling with things for a while before that?

Functioning normally? Oh, yeah, absolutely. Everything was completely fine until about a year ago. That's when my dad's medical issues started getting worse and he had to start getting all these frequent labs and going to a million appointments. That's when I first started noticing the numbers being altered. 

Before that, everything was great. Work was fine, my personal life was fine. I actually had a lot more free time before all these appointments started. I used to go to this pottery class on Tuesday nights. It was so relaxing, just working with the clay. Although, the instructor, Brenda, was a little intense. She would hover over your shoulder and critique every little thing. "Your walls are too thick, your base isn't centered." It's like, Brenda, I'm making a bowl for my keys, not a masterpiece for the Louvre. She always wore these huge, chunky turquoise necklaces, too. Like, three of them at a time. They would clank against the pottery wheels when she leaned over. It drove me crazy. I actually stopped going because she kept trying to get everyone to buy into this essential oil pyramid scheme she was running on the side. She said peppermint oil could cure my dad's kidney issues. Can you believe that? Peppermint oil. As if I don't know how the renal system works. I draw blood for BUN and creatinine every single day. 

But yeah, before a year ago, when all this lab stuff started with my dad, everything was completely normal. I was doing just fine.

Over this past year, have you had any periods where you felt unusually happy, energetic, or like you could do anything—maybe sleeping only a few hours a night but still feeling great? Or has your mood been pretty stable the whole time?

Unusually happy? No, not really. My mood has been pretty stable, honestly. I mean, I've been stressed about my dad and the lab results, obviously, but I haven't had any weird bursts of energy or stopped sleeping. I always try to get my full eight hours. Sleep is so important, you know? If I don't sleep, I get terrible bags under my eyes. 

I actually tried this new eye cream last month to help with the dark circles. It was supposed to have caffeine and hyaluronic acid in it. I bought it at Sephora, and the girl working there was so pushy. She kept trying to get me to buy the matching night serum, which was like eighty dollars. Eighty dollars for a tiny little pump bottle! And the pump didn't even work right on the tester. It just kind of sputtered and shot lotion onto the mirror. It reminded me of the hand sanitizer dispenser in the waiting room at our clinic. The maintenance guy, Carl, filled it with this cheap, watery sanitizer instead of the gel we usually get, and now every time a patient uses it, it just sprays all over the floor. It's a huge slipping hazard. I almost wiped out in my Crocs the other day. I love my Crocs, though. They're the only shoes that don't make my arches ache after standing for an eight-hour shift. I have these little Jibbitz on them—one is a syringe and the other is a little red blood drop. My niece gave them to me for my birthday. She's seven, and she's going through this huge dinosaur phase right now. Everything is T-Rex this and Triceratops that. 

But anyway, no, I haven't had any weird energetic phases or anything. Just my normal self.

When you first looked at your dad's lab results a year ago and thought something was wrong, did you have that concern right away from that very first time you saw them, or did it take several weeks or months of looking at multiple lab results before you became convinced they were being changed?

Right away? Well, let me think. When I first looked at them, I mean, I know what BUN and creatinine levels are supposed to look like for someone his age and with his history. I draw these labs all day. It's like second nature to me. You see the numbers, and you just know. But when I saw his, it was... wait, did it happen right away? 

I think I noticed it immediately, yeah. Because the numbers just didn't make sense. And the font on the printout looked slightly different, too. It's like they used Arial instead of Calibri, and the hospital always uses Calibri. Always. I remember when they switched the system over three years ago, the IT guy, Dave, made this huge deal about how Calibri is easier to read on screens. Dave is such a character. He always wears these faded graphic tees with old video game logos on them, like Pac-Man or Atari. He told me once he has a whole room in his house just for his vintage arcade machines. His wife must hate that. My ex-boyfriend tried to do something like that with his comic books, just taking over the entire guest room. It smelled like old paper and dust all the time. I tried getting him to put a dehumidifier in there, but he said the noise bothered him while he was reading. Which is ridiculous because he used to fall asleep with the TV blaring infomercials at two in the morning. I can't stand infomercials. Those ones for the non-stick pans where they burn cheese in them? Who burns cheese on purpose? 

Anyway, yeah, I noticed it right away on that first printout. It didn't take weeks. I saw it that very first time.

Looking back over your entire life before this year—say, five or ten years ago—did you ever have any other situations where you were absolutely certain about something that other people around you didn't believe or couldn't see, even when they told you that you were wrong?

Other situations? Like, where people thought I was wrong? No, no, I've never had anything like that. I've always been pretty grounded. People usually come to me for advice, honestly, because I'm so practical. Like my sister, she's always asking me what to do about her kids. 

She has three boys, and they are just wild. The middle one, Leo, he decided last week that he wanted to cut his own hair. He found these kitchen shears—the really heavy-duty ones that you use for cutting through poultry bones. I have a pair just like them from Williams Sonoma. They were a gift from my aunt when I moved into my first apartment. She also got me this beautiful Dutch oven, but it's so heavy I can barely lift it out of the cabinet. I tried making a beef stew in it once, but I left it on the stove too long and the bottom scorched. It took me three days to scrub it clean. I had to use so much baking soda and vinegar, it smelled like a science fair volcano in my kitchen. 

You know, I actually won second place in the science fair in seventh grade. I did a whole project on capillary action in celery. You put the stalks in food coloring and watch the water travel up the tubes. It's fascinating. The girl who won first place, Melissa, her dad was an engineer, so he basically built her entire project for her. It was this working model of a hydroelectric dam. So unfair. She wore these awful butterfly hair clips every single day. 

But no, to answer your question, I've never had anything like what you're talking about before this year. Just this thing with the labs.

Has there ever been any other time in your life—even briefly—when you were certain about something that turned out not to be true, or when you believed something strongly that nobody else around you could understand or agree with?

No, I mean, you just asked me that, right? I've never had any other time like that. Like I said, I'm a very practical person. I don't just go around making things up or believing crazy things. I stick to the facts. Blood draws, lab results, things you can see and measure. 

Measuring things reminds me, I actually need to get a new measuring cup. The one I have, the little red lines on the glass have completely faded off from going through the dishwasher so many times. It's Pyrex, which you'd think would hold up better, but I guess the detergent I use is just too harsh. I switched to those little pods a few months ago because they were on sale at Costco. I love Costco. You go in for dishwasher pods and you come out with a rotisserie chicken, a three-pack of sweatpants, and a kayak. I don't even know how to kayak. My friend Sarah tried to get me to go paddleboarding with her last summer on the lake, but the water looked so murky. I kept thinking about all the bacteria in there. You know, Naegleria fowleri? The brain-eating amoeba? It lives in warm freshwater. We learned about it in one of my intro bio classes. The professor was this really intense guy who always wore bow ties. He looked exactly like Bill Nye, but without the sense of humor. He failed half the class on the midterm. I passed, though. Barely, but I passed. 

But yeah, no. I've never believed anything that wasn't true before. Just the lab results, because I know what I saw.

Over this past year while you've been concerned about the lab results, have there been times when you felt completely normal and didn't think about the lab changes at all, or has this concern been pretty much constant in your mind every single day?

Well, it's been going on for about a year now. Pretty much ever since my dad's medical issues started and he needed all those frequent labs and appointments. It's been constant, honestly. I mean, how could I not think about it? Every time I look at a screen, I'm checking the font. 

Speaking of fonts, I actually started looking into typography online. Did you know there's a whole documentary about the font Helvetica? It's wild. People get so passionate about letters. I tried to watch it on a Sunday afternoon, but my neighbor decided to start using his leaf blower right outside my window. He does this every Sunday. And he doesn't even have that many trees! It's just a few maples, but he acts like he's clearing a whole forest. He wears these heavy-duty earmuffs, too, the kind you see guys wearing on the tarmac at airports. I've always wondered what it would be like to work at an airport, you know? The smell of jet fuel, watching people reunite at baggage claim. I love baggage claim. It's like a real-life soap opera sometimes. I saw a couple get into a huge fight once because the guy grabbed the wrong black suitcase. It was a Samsonite, and everyone has a black Samsonite. You really have to put a ribbon or something on it. I use a bright yellow luggage tag shaped like a pineapple. 

But yeah, to answer your question, it's been pretty much every day for the last year. I don't really have days where I just forget about it, because they're always messing with his results.

Before this year when the lab concerns started, would people who knew you well—like family or close friends—say that you were the same person you are now, or do you think they might say you've changed as a person in some fundamental way?

Well, I think they'd say I'm exactly the same. Outside of this whole dispute about my dad's records, I mean, nothing has changed. I still keep all my phlebotomy shifts at the clinic. I pay my bills on time, I take care of myself, I manage all my normal day-to-day responsibilities. 

Speaking of responsibilities, I actually had to take my car in for an oil change yesterday. It's a Honda Civic, and they are usually so reliable, but the little maintenance light has been glaring at me for three weeks. The waiting room at the mechanic's shop was freezing. They had the AC blasting, and it's barely spring outside. I had to sit there for an hour reading a magazine from 2019. It had an article about organizing your pantry with clear plastic bins. I tried doing that once, the whole Home Edit thing? I bought like twenty bins from Target. It looked great for about a week, but then I went grocery shopping and none of the new boxes would fit right, so I just ended up stacking things on top of the bins. It's a total mess now. My cat, Barnaby, he likes to sleep on top of the fridge, and sometimes he bats the cereal boxes down. He knocked over a brand new box of Cheerios the other day. They went everywhere. Do you know how hard it is to sweep up Cheerios from under a refrigerator? You have to use the little crevice tool on the vacuum, but mine is missing. I think I left it at my old apartment when I moved. 

But yeah, my friends and family, they wouldn't say I've changed fundamentally or anything. I'm still just me, doing my job and living my life. It's just the lab thing that's different.

If I were to tell you that I reviewed your dad's lab results myself with one of the doctors here, and we both confirmed that the numbers are actually correct and haven't been changed, would you be able to consider that maybe you could have misremembered what the original numbers were, or would you still be completely certain that they were altered?

No, I wouldn't. I mean, with all due respect, I know what I saw. I'm a phlebotomist, I look at these numbers all day, every day. I know the chart doesn't match what I originally saw. I've spent the whole last year trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or holding back parts of his results. And honestly, it doesn't matter how many doctors or family members tell me the numbers are fine, because I know they're not. It's just... it's really wearing me down, to be honest. 

It's like trying to get a straight answer out of my cable company. Have you ever tried to call customer service for your internet? It is a nightmare. I was on hold for forty-five minutes last Tuesday just to ask why my bill went up twelve dollars. They play this awful elevator music, but it's really staticky, and every three minutes a recorded voice comes on and says, "Your call is very important to us." If it's so important, why am I waiting forty-five minutes? And then when you finally get a person, they talk to you like you're an idiot. The guy asked me if I had tried unplugging my router. Of course I unplugged the router! That's the first thing you do. It's like the universal fix for everything. Just turn it off and turn it back on again. My dad used to say that about the lawnmower, actually. We had this old Toro mower when I was a kid, and it was so stubborn. You had to pull the cord like ten times to get it to start. My arm would be so sore by the time I actually got to mow the lawn. I hated mowing the lawn. The grass clippings always got stuck to my ankles and made me itch. I'm actually mildly allergic to grass, which is ironic, right? 

But yeah, no. I wouldn't consider that I misremembered. Because I didn't. I know exactly what I saw on those labs.

In that first week or two when you first noticed the lab results were being changed, did everything feel completely normal otherwise—like your thoughts were clear and you were sleeping and functioning fine—or did you feel like something was off or strange about how you were experiencing the world in general?

Everything was completely normal. I was sleeping fine, my thoughts were clear, I was just doing my normal routine. Actually, I was sleeping really well right around then because I had just bought this new memory foam mattress topper. It was one of those ones with the blue cooling gel swirls in it? I got it at Target. Well, I say I got a deal, but honestly, I think they just mark up the original price so the sale price looks better. My friend Sarah used to work in retail, and she said they do that all the time. She worked at this little boutique downtown that sold these tiny, flimsy scarves for like eighty dollars. Who pays eighty dollars for a scarf? Unless it's cashmere, maybe. I've never owned anything cashmere. It seems like it would be really high maintenance. You probably have to hand wash it in the sink with special soap. I hate hand washing things. I usually just throw everything in on the delicate cycle and hope for the best. My washing machine has this weird quirk where it gets stuck on the spin cycle and just keeps spinning and spinning until you physically go over and push the button to stop it. It makes this loud thumping noise, like someone is bowling in my laundry room. I should probably get the landlord to look at it. 

But anyway, yeah, nothing felt off or strange about the world or anything like that. I was functioning perfectly fine. It was just the shock of seeing that someone had altered my dad's chart.

If you went back and looked at your dad's original lab results right now today, and they matched exactly what the doctors are showing you, what would you think—would that change your mind about whether they were altered, or would you think something else was going on?

If they matched right now? Honestly, I would just think they went deeper into the system and altered the original files, too. Like I said a few minutes ago, I have spent this entire past year trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or holding back parts of my dad’s lab results. And I know I sound like a broken record, but no matter how many doctors or family members tell me the numbers are fine, I know the chart doesn’t match what I originally saw. They can show me a hundred pieces of paper, but it won't change my mind, and fighting this is just really wearing me down. It is so exhausting. 

Because changing a computer file is so easy, you know? It’s just hitting backspace. My keyboard at work is actually missing the backspace key right now. Well, not missing, but the little plastic cap popped off, so you just have to press the little rubber squishy nub underneath to delete anything. It is so annoying. I put in a work order with IT like two months ago. The IT guy, I think his name is Greg, he came down and looked at it, and then he just said he had to order a whole new keyboard. How hard is it to find a standard keyboard? They sell them at Best Buy for like fifteen dollars. 

I was actually at Best Buy last weekend looking for a new charger for my phone because Barnaby—my cat—chewed through the cord again. He loves chewing on wires. I had to buy those little plastic cord protector tubes to put over all my cables, but they are so ugly. They look exactly like those old coiled telephone cords from the nineties. Remember those? My grandma had a bright yellow one in her kitchen that could stretch all the way into the dining room. She used to talk on the phone and cook at the same time, making these huge pots of spaghetti sauce. She'd let it simmer all day long. The whole house would smell like garlic and tomatoes. I tried making her recipe once, but I burned the garlic. Once you burn garlic, the whole dish is ruined, you just have to throw it away and start over. 

But no, seeing a piece of paper wouldn't change my mind. I know what I saw on his chart, and they're just covering their tracks.

Over this past year since you first noticed the lab results were changed, has your certainty about this stayed exactly the same the whole time, or has there been periods where you felt more convinced or less convinced about it at different points?

No, it hasn't changed at all. I've been completely certain from day one. I know I keep repeating myself, but it's because for the entire past year I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or holding back parts of my dad’s lab results. And no matter how many doctors or family members tell me the numbers are fine, I know the chart doesn’t match what I saw. I've never doubted that, not for a single second. But it’s wearing me down. It is just so exhausting. 

I feel like I really need a vacation to get away from it all for a few days. Have you ever been to Sedona? My cousin went to Sedona last spring and she said the red rocks are just beautiful. She brought me back this little cactus in a painted ceramic pot, but I accidentally overwatered it and it died. Cacti are supposed to be the easiest plants in the world to take care of, but I always manage to kill them. I think I just hover too much. I'm a hoverer. 

Even when I bake cookies, I pull up a chair right in front of the oven door and just watch them bake through the glass. I don't even set a timer anymore. I just watch them until the edges get perfectly golden brown. You have to take them out right exactly then, or they get too crunchy. I absolutely hate crunchy chocolate chip cookies. They should be soft and chewy in the middle, you know? My mom used to make the best cookies, and she'd put a slice of plain white sandwich bread in the Tupperware container to keep them soft. It actually works perfectly, the cookies absorb the moisture from the bread. Science is weird like that. 

But yeah, my certainty hasn't wavered at all. I know exactly what I saw.

My arm would be so sore by the time I actually got to mow the lawn. I hated mowing the lawn. The grass clippings always got stuck to my ankles and made me itch.
